title: Central Pennsylvania & Catskills
original_caption:
Just took a brief driving trip through central PA and NY Catskills over 5 days. Low key through a lot of small towns! 
1. Gettysburg: the key turning point battle of the US Civil War, over 3 days in 1863. The battle strategy, the casualties (50K) with loss of life (11K), and the morale boost to the Union for the remainder of the war, and Lincoln�??s 2 minute address at the newly created national cemetery (Forescore, 7 years�?�). We did the auto audio tour of the 25 mile battlefield. 

2. Corning: the history of glass over the years, and innovations leading to the current fiberoptic era (from tele/microscopes, medical instruments to AI) was revelatory. 

3. Cooperstown: lovely quaint town on the Otsego lake where the Susquehanna river begins (and flows through Philadelphia to Baltimore) is all things baseball! the compact hall of fame museum, Doubleday field, and endless streams of little league baseball tournaments, and paraphernalia! 

4. Storm King Art Center: in the middle of nowhere is a 500 acre outdoor museum of sculpture where you can spend a whole day! 

These areas require a driving commitment to reach but well worth the effort!

title: Grand Tetons, Yellowstone & Glacier
original_caption:
Just completed a 2-week trip out west in mid-September (Jackson Hole, Grand Tetons, Yellowstone, and Glacier national parks), flew in and out of Salt Lake City and rented a car. Lots of driving, weather was beautiful, the trees were starting to turn, but have not peaked, and crowds were not crazy. There is a lot of money in the Jackson Hole area! 

Each of the parks had their own character, and I have seen my share of geysers, wildlife, stunning mountains, waterfalls, and rivers! The geysers and thermal events were other-worldly, but Glacier was special, with the Road-to-the-Sun!  We used a narration app (Action Tour Guide) linked to GPS to provide background on various areas and worked nicely for a self-paced driving tour. 

The Grand Tetons is a smaller NP, with a central loop around Jackson Lake and the smaller but iconic Jenny Lake, with great bike trails (Moose-Wilson Rd, Oxbow bend, Antelope flats, Kelly loop, Elk refuge). We stayed outside Jackson in a roadside motel (functional for $400/night!). The backdrop of the stark Tenons is ever present!  

Yellowstone is a massive park 50 X 40 miles, with 4 separate entrances. We stayed in Gardiner near the northern entrance. The grand loop forming a figure 8 helps to organize the key areas, from the Mammoth Hot Springs, stretching from Norris basin down to upper, middle, and lower basins that includes Old Faithful. Then to the east is the Yellowstone Lake, fishing bridge, mud pool, Lamar Valley rich in wildlife (bison and elk herds with occasional black bears along the Yellowstone River), and the Roosevelt Tower area. The interdependence of the wildlife, predator and prey, and the effect of humans both for good and ill becomes obvious. The geysers and the local geology are fascinating and educational, the interplay between massive forces that involve molten rock, ongoing supply of water, and a network of cracks and crevices to put on an ongoing show for the ages! You can see the emerging attraction for geo-thermal energy industry worldwide!

Glacier NP is a good 6-hour drive through Montana from YS NP. The west to east �??Road to the Sun�?? is the engineering marvel of the park, covering the eastern edge of Lake McDonald, continental divide and Logan�??s Pass at around 8500 feet. This scenic and hair-raising drive requires timed-entry and takes a minimum of 2-3 hours. There are many scenic lookouts and a variety of hikes from easy to strenuous!  The dramatic scenery is the focus of Glacier, not large wildlife. West Glacier and St Mary�??s are the two small towns at either end of park. Glacier has a very short season (July - September), as roads are snowed in!

The NPs have a variety of trails that meet the needs of all levels of tourists and hikers! There was enough free time baked in for us to wander into Missoula MT, Idaho Falls, and SLC (Park City, Olympic Village, and Temple Square). We stayed at a "hostel" near West Glacier (with a bunk bed and shared bathrooms, which worked surprisingly well!). Lodging was generally expensive, and we did not stay at any of the lodges in the parks (requires reservations well in advance of 12 months). 

Overall, another bucket-list trip! Here is the resultant "photo dump."

title: Montreal & Quebec City
original_caption:
I have completed a one-week journey (Philly-NYC-Montreal-Quebec City and return) with a 3-wheel electric scooter (Topmate ES-35), my wife, and 2 suitcases, all on trains, which proved to be an adventure. 

The Amtrak Adirondack from NYC to Montreal is an 11-hour ride with user-friendly amenities, featuring coach seating and a dining car ($75 per person each way). Montreal was delightful, particularly Old Montreal (Notre Dame cathedral, waterfront), neighborhoods like the Latin Quarter and Mount Royale Plateau, and the St. Lawrence Corridor. Unfortunately, we did miss the famed Montreal Jazz Festivale by 2 weeks. The subsequent 3-hour Canadian VIA rail journey was more pleasant than Amtrak. 

Quebec City exuded European charm with its 500-year history, culture, outdoor cafes, cobblestone streets, and hills in the old city. The Fairmont Le ChÃ¢teau Frontenac, surrounding Dufferin Terrace boardwalk, and numerous other attractions showcased old-world charm. Most notable in QC are the vast array of outdoor eateries, with streets blocked off for cars. We did a daytrip to Montmorency Falls (15 miles outside Quebec City), which is taller than Niagara, has a suspension bridge across the falls, lots of stairs, etc. Worth adding to one's bucket list; Despite recent weakness, $1 US equals $1.37 CN. Both cities were exceptionally clean, and the public sectors simply functioned well! Stark difference with US cities. Overwhelmingly French, but all hospitality staff were thoroughly bilingual.

The return trip was brutal (530a departure from QC and back home to Philly by 2a)! ð­

title: Alaska
original_caption:
Friends would like to report on our recent bucket list journey to Alaska, by both water and land that lasted about 3 weeks. Reasons to go to Alaska are for dramatic scenery with snow-capped mountains everywhere, geologic history with many glaciers from the last ice age, incredible wildlife on both water and land, history of migration of peoples (including "native Indians" over thousands of years, Russians in the 1700s, Klondike gold prospectors who were duped in 1890s), wayward recent transplants (both seasonal and permanent) there for some reason, and of course the tourists from all over the world (lots of Aussies and Kiwis). Learned about "Seward's Folly" as AK (twice the size of TX) was purchased from the Russians in 1867 (after the civil war) for $7M (2 cents an acre), for an "icebox" that proved to be great deal, as it became a state in 1959.

You don't go to Alaska for the weather, as it was cold (daytime 40s-50s F), frequently rainy with low clouds, and very changeable weather. Layered waterproof gear is a requirement.

We flew into Vancouver (YVR) for a few days, then boarded our first ever cruise (Holland America, Nordham, with 1800 passengers, or a mid-size cruiser) for 7 days via the "inner passage" or the "Alaskan maritime highway" where the ship is in sight of land on both sides. Day stops were in Ketchikan, Juneau, and Skagway, where we took a variety of land excursions (sponsored by the cruise company) to Saxman native village, Mendenhall glacier and whale watching, railroad to the White Pass noted for the Klondike gold era, and up close and personal views of Glacier Bay National Park with the College Fjords. All these areas are accessible only by boat (or small plane) as there are no direct roads. The cruise completed in Whittier, AK, where we boarded a bus to Anchorage and stopped at a local wildlife preserve (saw moose, caribou, fox, black bear, coyote, muskox). 

We rented a car and spent a few days each from Anchorage, Girdwood, Seward (took a catamaran to the Kenai Fjords National Park), Homer, Talkeetna, and Denali National Park. Wished we stayed another day or two in Denali. Then drove 5 hours back to Anchorage to take a red eye from ANC to IAD and PHL. Overall impressions: surreal; did not see darkness for 3 weeks; shell-shocked from the landscapes and memories, of both the animal type as well as the people type! Perspectives from travelers from outside the US were highly informative. 

Definitely a bucket list trip, esp. the combo of both water and land (organized as well as self-directed). Trip was highly educational as well as fun! Strongly recommend it. Advanced reservations are necessary for premium experiences (i.e. we could not get on the bus tour into Denali for the Tundra drive which goes deeper into the park than what we did), for certain lodges, hikes. The state flag has the big dipper and north star, and the state bird is willow ptarmigan and of course moose as the state animal.

title: Cross-country Amtrak
original_caption:
Riding the rails! Just returned from a x-country Amtrak train adventure, from Philly to Seattle. Bought a USA Rail pass ($499) which entitles you to 10 "legs" within 30 days, all coach seats anywhere in the US. I went from Philly to NYC (Moynihan Hall), then NYC to Chicago Union station (24 hours), and by the California Zephyr to Emeryville, CA (52 hours). The spectacular scenery over the snow-covered Rockies started in Denver to Grand Junction and then to Salt Lake City, and over the Sierras through Reno to Sacramento! After some downtime in Berkeley, the next leg was the Coastal Starlight from Emeryville to Seattle (King St station, 24 hours). The section around Eugene over the Cascades was spectacular. I deferred the return train journey, which was supposed to be the Empire Builder via the northern route from Seattle to Chicago (47 hours), in favor of a 5-hour Alaska Air flight, which was a miserable aisle seat (mistake)!

There are many things to be aware of for a journey like this. The trains on the east coast tend to be single-deckers, whereas the long-range westbound trains are double-deckers. The trains have a variety of seating and luxury options, from coach seating to private roomettes or rooms and first class. The coach seats (which could be on level 1 or 2) are perfectly adequate, 2 seats on each side (no middle seat) with a large picture window, very roomy recliner with lots of legroom, electric outlets and lots of storage. The Wi-Fi was spotty, especially in the rural areas. Most of the legs I did not have a seatmate! The seats are much roomier and comfortable than airline seats.

Now, how comfortable is a coach for overnight sleeping? Well, it depends on how easily you fall asleep, whether you can sleep in a recliner, etc. If you bring a blanket and a neck pillow, I did not find it too onerous! However, some might find it intolerable! The alternative is a small roomette (where seats can be configured to 2 bunk beds), which are 3-5X the cost of a coach seat or a larger room (7-10X coach), but meals are included! The double-deckers have a dedicated observation deck, available to coach seats as well, with swivel seats, tables, couches with large picture windows extending to the ceilings. In addition, there is a dining car for sit down meal service (breakfast $20, lunch $30, and dinner $40). Alternative is a cafe car for snacks. The Amtrak staff were extremely helpful and readily available. The Amtrak app is very user-friendly, though it was down on several occasions, so back-up screenshots of tickets is important!  Personal safety etc. was not an issue on any of the trains or stations. 

Of course, the journey can be the destination as it was for me! The fellow travelers were a mix between folks like me (looking for an adventure with time on their hands, both young and old) or folks looking for shorter legs to get somewhere. This is an unusual way to travel, without the stress of driving, gorgeous and varied scenery coast to coast, with a lot of down time to meditate (or read a book or listen to something). Of course, if you are into trains there is a lot of history for the transcontinental railroads, west-ward expansion, from coal-powered steam engines to construction of tracks through the Rockies with a variety of tunnels at altitude (i.e. Donner pass), small towns, etc. A perk is casual conversations with folks from all walks of life and geographic regions!  I learned about varied reefer laws across the states as well as debated the recent election results! 

I would highly encourage this way of seeing America, at least once, either on the cheap or in some luxury depending on your mood and means! 

https://amtrakguide.com/routes/california-zephyr/

title: Utah National Parks
original_caption: Dear friends, just returned from a 2-week road trip to Utah's "mighty five" national parks; was an "other worldly" landscape unlike anything I have experienced before! We flew from Philly into Vegas and rented an AWD Ford Edge and drove 1100 miles, clockwise, to Zion NP, Bryce Canyon, Capitol Reef NP, Canyonlands, Arches NP / Moab, Monument Valley, Grand Canyon and back to Vegas. Late sept was a great time, both weather and crowds (mostly Europeans). The trip was ambitious with a lot of schlepping, our 4-6 mos. lead time was not enough to stay in the NP lodges! the landscape, geologic history, and night sky were dramatic and awe-inspiring! For the highly fit, there is tremendous opportunity for hiking (the "narrows at Zion or Navajo trail at Bryce, biking in many places, etc. I travelled with an electric trike and had great access to a variety of trails, vistas, etc. Also, did a 4-hour white-knuckle drive on the Shafer trail in Canyonlands (not for faint-of-heart) and a jeep tribal tour of monument valley. I attempted a drone video with limited success (prohibited in most national and public parks). Would highly recommend, even a portion, for anyone!

title: Greece
original_caption:
Friends, we just returned from an ambitious 2-week Greek Odyssey! Overall, it was spectacular, exhausting, and other-worldly; Greece has a reputation for being rugged, hilly and not being friendly for "accessible travel"; however, we found ways to explore broadly from Athens to the length of Crete to Santorini; the more you prepare the more you can get out of an international trip in such a historic place with ruins, villages built on top of ruins and cliff sides, etc! We had assistance from a travel specialist focused on Greece (Sabine Switalla, Care Under the Sun), which added a layer of support. The motivation for this trip came from a friend of mine Mel Karas, whom I wish to thank. 
We did document our trip in an innovative way on a cool travel app called Esplor.io which collates your journey by using GPS locaton and maps, photos you take, and any diary comments you make that is readily sharable with family and frends (in almost real time); I highly recommend it and will utilize for future travel.
Like all great trips, you want to go back and see and read more! Highly recommend Greece.

title: The Ringling Museum and Sarasota History
original_caption:
Sarasota FL has a very interesting history at the turn of the last century (1880 - 1920). The Ringling Brothers, from Baraboo, WI, popularized the traveling 3-ring circus in the US. John Ringling, the consummate entrepreneur, developed the complex logistics for creating makeshift tent cities overnight to put on these shows involving hundreds of people and animals. These were temporary outfits that moved from town to town in caravans, to later include railroads.  This was a major form of entertainment for several decades with stunts, high-wire acts, clowns, spectacle for everyone. The Ringling Brothers contributed greatly to many innovations in logistics, building tent cities, supply chains, management.  The US Army actually took away important lessons in these early days of automobile.

As Ringling made his money, he diversified into railroads, real estate, and oil and became famously rich. He bought up hundreds of acres in Sarasota FL extending to Longboat key and Lido beach. He built a sprawling winter home resort for the elites of the era. He was a major collector of art. The Ca'd'Zan is the house that John built is an opulent Venetian Gothic-style museum. This complex is on the bay, together with a fine art museum with many works from Reubens and other European artists along with a learning center for the history of the circus and massive model of the circus. 

The circus has given us many words to our lexicon: 3-ring circus, side show, step-right-up, clown show, ringmaster, "big top", bandwagon, "come in", etc.  Ringling initially partnered with Barnum and Bailey and then bought them out to consolidate his grip. Eventually, with advances in other entertainment forms such as the radio, TV, and film together with the 1927 FL real estate bust and the stock market crash and the Great Depression, brought an end to the traveling circus by the 1950s.  John died in 1936.

I did not know about the Ringling legacy or this history till our recent trip. It is fascinating and is worth a definite visit, as a respite from the usual FL beach trip.

title: Mote Aquarium, Sarasota
original_caption:
Just visited the Mote Aquarium (near UTC in Sarasota), blown away by their "model", not only great for the casual visitor, but for their research and training functions to attract future conservationists and scientists. They use lab techniques to generate jellyfish and other species and rescue injured sea animals for rehab.  The exhibits were highly immersive and interactive, with many separate glass-enclosed chambers to get up close to sharks, natural coral reefs, etc. The Sea Netter was my favorite!
https://mote.org/aquarium/
